title: Secular institutes
hookLine: consecrated people living ordinary jobs in the world

lines: THE GUARD, THE ACCOUNTANT, THE SHOPKEEPER.
cards: The security guard on the night shift. The accountant two desks over. The woman who runs the hardware store and remembers which screws you bought last time.
Any of them could have made vows of poverty, chastity and obedience, and you would never know. No habit, no convent, no title on the name badge.
They pay rent, file taxes, go to the office party, and live a consecration the Church recognizes. Today, a calling designed to be hard to spot.

teach.b: First, the name. A secular institute is a form of consecrated life, but secular here doesn't mean unbelieving. It means in the world, in ordinary time and ordinary places.

teach.h: VOWS, LIVED AT HOME AND AT WORK.
teach.b: The Code of Canon Law describes these institutes as groups whose members, living in the world, strive for the perfection of charity and work to make the world holy, especially from within. From within is the key phrase.

Members commit to the evangelical counsels, poverty, chastity and obedience, by the bonds each institute sets, but they live in the ordinary conditions of the world: alone, with their families, or in small groups.
Some institutes are for laypeople, some for priests. A lay member stays a layperson; a priest member stays a diocesan priest. Then the picture.
Jesus told a parable about bread.

teach.h: LIKE LEAVEN HIDDEN IN THE DOUGH.
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "The kingdom of heaven is like to leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of meal, until the whole was leavened." Notice the word hid. Yeast doesn't sit on top of the dough looking holy.
It disappears into it, and the whole loaf changes. The Code uses the same picture: these members act like leaven. Last, the quiet.
Some institutes ask members to keep their consecration private, so they can work anywhere, as colleagues rather than visitors.

teach.h: THE WITNESS IS THE WORK ITSELF.
teach.b: Their witness is the work itself: a fair invoice, an unhurried hour with a difficult patient, a meeting run honestly.
Yesterday's hermits went out to the edges. These people stay in the middle of everything, and the point is that nobody notices.

how: Members of secular institutes make a commitment to poverty, chastity and obedience while keeping ordinary jobs and homes. They usually wear no habit, and some institutes ask members to keep their consecration private.

o: consecrated life lived in the world, from within
non-religious charities run by the Catholic Church

p: how they make the world holy

s: in the Code, secular means living in the world, in its ordinary conditions.

games.q: you've made vows in a secular institute. a colleague asks what you did last weekend. what does your calling ask of you?
o: live it in the work, quietly, as your institute asks.
games.why: secular institutes are lived from within the world, like leaven hidden in dough. some ask members to keep the consecration private.

practice: You may not know anyone who has made these vows, and that's the point. Let your mind walk through the places you pass in a week, a clinic, a classroom, an office, a shop, where someone may be living a hidden promise.
If you pray, ask God to strengthen them, whoever they are; if you don't, wish them well, and let the faces you pass feel a little less ordinary.

wordCard.voice: Secular institutes. Consecrated life lived in the world, from within, like yeast in the dough. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, leaven: the yeast in Jesus's parable, hidden in the meal until the whole is leavened.

carryVoice: Your line: hidden in the world. Like yeast in the dough: unseen, and the whole loaf changes. Go gently.
